questions.stem: The Riemann hypothesis states that all non-trivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$ have real part equal to:

options.explanation: All non-trivial zeros are conjectured to lie on the critical line $\text{Re}(s) = 1/2$. This is unproved; over $10^{13}$ zeros have been verified numerically to lie there.
$\zeta(s)$ has a simple pole at $s=1$ and no zeros near $\text{Re}(s) = 1$. The prime number theorem uses the zero-free region near this line.
$\text{Re}(s) = 0$ is on the boundary of the critical strip but not the conjectured location of zeros.
The trivial zeros are at $s = -2, -4, -6, \ldots$ (even negative integers). The Riemann hypothesis concerns the non-trivial zeros, which lie in the critical strip $0 < \text{Re}(s) < 1$.

questions.stem: The prime number theorem asserts that $\pi(x)$, the number of primes up to $x$, satisfies:

options.explanation: Proved by Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin in 1896 using the properties of the Riemann zeta function. The logarithmic integral $\text{Li}(x)$ is a better approximation.
The prime counting function grows much faster than $\sqrt{x}$. For $x = 10^6$, $\pi(x) = 78498$ while $\sqrt{10^6} = 1000$.
If $\pi(x) \sim x$, essentially every integer would be prime. The actual density of primes near $x$ is approximately $1/\log x$.
Off by one factor of $\log x$. The correct asymptotic is $x / \log x$.

questions.stem: Euler's product formula $\zeta(s) = \prod_p (1-p^{-s})^{-1}$ is equivalent to:

options.text: The fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every integer has a unique prime factorisation.
options.explanation: Expanding the Euler product and collecting terms gives $\sum n^{-s}$ precisely because each $n$ appears exactly once, from its unique factorisation into primes. The product formula IS the analytic form of unique factorisation.
The Euler product is a formal identity; proving the PNT requires deep analysis of zeros of $\zeta(s)$, far beyond the product formula alone.
The Euler product is a proved identity. The Riemann hypothesis is an unproved conjecture about zeros of $\zeta$.

options.text: Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions.
options.explanation: Dirichlet's theorem requires L-functions (generalisations of $\zeta$). The Euler product alone does not give Dirichlet's theorem.
